plan: Literary narrative of about 520 words (CLD-P-ACT-R-000021) about a grandson finding his grandfather's uncollected IOUs; eight items labelled easy or medium per the verbal-labelling note.

passages.title: The Bottom Drawer
passages.text:
Theo arrived at the hardware store on the last Saturday before the sale. The shelves were half empty, and the light through the front window fell on rows of bare pegboard. His grandmother, Ruth, was moving down an aisle with a roll of masking tape and a marker, writing prices on the tape and pressing it onto bins of screws and hinges. "Everything goes," she said when she saw him, "except what nobody wants."

She gave him the counter. For forty years his grandfather had stood behind it, and its drawers held what Theo expected: rubber bands, pencil stubs, a stapler, receipt books gone soft at the corners. In the bottom drawer, under a tangle of string, he found a cigar box. Inside were slips of paper in his grandfather's square handwriting. "Owe 2 hinges, R. Malloy." "Paint, 1 gal., Delgado, pay Friday." "Chain saw blade, Pruitt, after harvest." Some were dated, the oldest more than thirty years back. There were forty-one of them, and not one had been crossed out.

Theo added them up on the back of a receipt. Eight hundred twelve dollars and forty cents. He had always thought of his grandfather as a careful man, the kind who sorted every bolt by size and could tell you, without looking, which drawer held the quarter-inch washers. He carried the box to the back of the store, half expecting his grandmother to be angry, or at least embarrassed.

Ruth read three slips, then a fourth, and laughed. "He knew," she said. "He always knew." Malloy's barn had burned the year of the hinges. The Delgados had six children and a truck that broke down every winter. "Your grandfather thought writing it down was nearly the same as being paid," she said. "It meant he'd noticed."

Theo asked whether they should try to collect now, with the store closing and the bills still coming. Ruth closed the lid and put the box into her purse, not on the pile of things to be sold. "Some of these people will be at the sale," she said. "I'd like them to find the prices fair." Theo looked down the aisle at the strips of masking tape. Every price on them was lower than he would have guessed.

candidates.stem: Which of the following best describes the main focus of the passage?

choices.A: A young man helps his grandmother collect money that customers have owed the family store for decades.
choices.B: A grandmother explains to her grandson why the family hardware store is being forced to close.
choices.C: A young man discovers that his grandfather kept careless records of the store's inventory.
choices.D: A young man learns something unexpected about his grandfather through a box of unpaid debts and sees his grandmother carry on the same attitude.

candidates.explanation: The story centers on the IOU slips, what they reveal about the grandfather's kindness, and Ruth's choice to keep prices low for the same customers.

A.rationale: Ruth decides not to collect the debts.

B.rationale: The passage never explains why the store is closing.

C.rationale: The grandfather is described as careful about inventory; the slips show generosity, not carelessness.

hints: What discovery drives the story, and how does it end?

strategy.explanation: Summarize the beginning, middle and end before choosing.

candidates.remember: The main focus of a narrative covers its central discovery and its resolution.

candidates.stem: According to the passage, the cigar box contained:

choices.A: receipts for supplies the store had bought from other businesses.
choices.B: price labels made of masking tape for the upcoming sale.
choices.C: handwritten notes recording goods that customers had not yet paid for.
choices.D: letters that the grandfather had written to Ruth over thirty years.

candidates.evidence: Inside were slips of paper in his grandfather's square handwriting.
candidates.explanation: The slips say things like "Owe 2 hinges, R. Malloy": notes of goods customers took without paying.

A.rationale: The slips record what customers owed, not the store's purchases.

B.rationale: Ruth is writing the labels; they are not in the box.

D.rationale: The slips are short notes about debts, not letters.

hints: Reread the examples of the slips.
candidates.remember: Detail questions are answered by the text.

candidates.stem: It can most reasonably be inferred that when Theo brought the box to Ruth, he believed that she would:

choices.A: be upset that her husband had let so much money go uncollected.
choices.B: already know about the box and its contents.
choices.C: want to throw the slips away before the sale.
choices.D: ask him to add up the amount owed.

candidates.evidence: half expecting his grandmother to be angry, or at least embarrassed
candidates.explanation: The passage says Theo was "half expecting his grandmother to be angry, or at least embarrassed" about the uncollected debts.

B.rationale: Theo is surprised by her reaction; nothing suggests he expected her to know.

C.rationale: Nothing in the passage suggests this expectation.

D.rationale: Theo has already added it up himself.

hints: What does the passage say Theo was "half expecting"?
candidates.remember: An inference must be backed by a specific line.

candidates.stem: Ruth's reaction to the slips is best described as:
candidates.evidence: Ruth read three slips, then a fourth, and laughed.
candidates.explanation: Ruth laughs, says "He always knew," and explains that writing the debts down meant he had noticed people's hardships: amusement and admiration.

A.rationale: These are the reactions Theo expected, not the ones Ruth shows.

C.rationale: Ruth laughs and calmly puts the box away.

D.rationale: She reads the slips carefully and explains what they meant.

hints: What does Ruth do and say when she reads the slips?

strategy.explanation: Eliminate attitudes that contradict her laugh and her explanation.

candidates.remember: Infer attitude from both actions and words.

candidates.subskill: Meaning of a word in context
candidates.stem: As it is used in paragraph 4, the word "noticed" most nearly means that the grandfather had:

choices.A: recognized the hardships his customers were facing.
choices.B: seen the slips again when he opened the drawer.
choices.C: written a formal announcement about the debts.
choices.D: realized that the store was losing money.

candidates.evidence: Malloy's barn had burned the year of the hinges.
candidates.explanation: Ruth links the slips to customers' troubles (a burned barn, six children, a broken truck): writing them down meant he recognized those hardships.

B.rationale: Ruth means he paid attention to people, not that he saw the slips.

C.rationale: "Notice" can mean an announcement, but that meaning does not fit.

D.rationale: Ruth's examples are about customers' troubles, not the store's finances.

hints: What examples does Ruth give just before this line?

strategy.explanation: Replace "noticed" with your own phrase based on Ruth's examples.

candidates.remember: Use the surrounding examples to fix a word's meaning.

candidates.stem: The detail that the grandfather "sorted every bolt by size" (paragraph 3) mainly serves to:

choices.A: explain why the store's shelves were half empty before the sale.
choices.B: suggest that the grandfather cared more about inventory than about customers.
choices.C: prove that the grandfather kept accurate records of every sale.
choices.D: show why Theo is surprised that the debts were never collected.

candidates.evidence: He had always thought of his grandfather as a careful man
candidates.explanation: Theo thought of his grandfather as careful, so forty-one uncollected debts seem out of character. The bolt detail sets up that surprise.

A.rationale: The empty shelves are unrelated to his sorting habits.

B.rationale: Ruth's explanation shows he cared about customers.

C.rationale: The uncollected slips show the opposite of strict record-keeping about payment.

hints: What did Theo believe about his grandfather before finding the box?

strategy.explanation: Ask what the detail sets up for the reader.

candidates.remember: Details about a character often set up a contrast with what comes next.

candidates.stem: The final sentence of the passage most strongly suggests that Ruth:

choices.A: had made errors when writing the prices on the tape.
choices.B: planned to raise the prices once the customers arrived.
choices.C: had set low prices, in keeping with her husband's generosity toward customers.
choices.D: knew that most of the items would not sell.

candidates.evidence: "I'd like them to find the prices fair."
candidates.explanation: Ruth wants the customers to find the prices fair, and every price is lower than Theo expected: she is continuing her husband's generosity.

A.rationale: Nothing suggests mistakes; her comment about fair prices implies the low prices were deliberate.

B.rationale: She says she wants the prices to seem fair, not that she will raise them.

D.rationale: The passage does not suggest she expects items to go unsold.

hints: What does Ruth say just before Theo looks at the tape?

strategy.explanation: Connect Ruth's last line to the final sentence.

candidates.remember: An ending often confirms what a character's last words imply.

candidates.subskill: Meaning of a phrase in context
candidates.stem: In paragraph 1, when Ruth says "Everything goes," she most nearly means that everything:

choices.D: will be moved to a new store.

candidates.evidence: writing prices on the tape and pressing it onto bins
candidates.explanation: Ruth is pricing items for the sale, so "everything goes" means everything will be sold.

A.rationale: She is pricing items for a sale, not discarding them.

C.rationale: "Anything goes" means anything is allowed, but that meaning does not fit a store sale.

D.rationale: The store is closing; nothing suggests a move.

hints: What is Ruth doing when she says this?

strategy.explanation: Use what she is doing to interpret the phrase.

candidates.remember: Read informal phrases in light of the scene.
